lessons.title: Caregiver burnout: caring for the carer

scenes.text: Rashmi, 46, in Nagpur cares for her mother after a stroke while working full time and raising two teenagers.
She sleeps four hours a night, snaps at everyone and feels guilty for even wanting a break.
Her brother in Dubai finally agrees to pay for a part-time attendant; her sister takes weekends; the teens help with meals.
Rashmi joins an online caregivers’ group and starts a 10-minute breathing practice. ‘I can care better when I’m not empty.’

steps.title: What burnout looks like
steps.body:
**Caregiver burnout** is physical, emotional and mental exhaustion from long-term caring. Signs:
- Constant tiredness, poor sleep
- Irritability, resentment, guilt
- Withdrawing from friends and hobbies
- Frequent illness, headaches
- Feeling hopeless or numb
It is common and **not a sign of weakness or lack of love**.

steps.title: Share the load
steps.body:
1. **List every task**: medicines, bathing, doctor visits, bills, cooking, night care, emotional support.
2. Hold a **family meeting** (video calls work) and divide tasks — including money and remote tasks (bookings, bills, calls) for those far away.
3. Use **paid help** where possible: part-time attendants, home nursing, day-care centres for elders.
4. Plan **respite**: regular breaks — a day a week, a weekend a month.
5. Write a simple **care plan** so anyone can step in.

steps.title: Small daily resets
steps.body:
- 10 minutes of slow breathing or a short walk
- Eating regular meals and drinking water
- One conversation a day that isn’t about caregiving
- Saying ‘no’ to non-essential demands
- Caregiver support groups (online or local) — people who understand reduce loneliness

steps.title: Get help when
steps.body: Seek support from a doctor or counsellor if you feel persistently low, anxious, hopeless, or are using alcohol or pills to cope. If you ever feel you might hurt yourself or the person you care for, reach out immediately: **Tele-MANAS 14416** or **112**. Asking for help protects both of you.

activity.label: Box breathing for carers: breathe in 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4

quiz.q: Caregiver burnout is…
options: A sign of not loving the person
quiz.why: Caregiver burnout is common exhaustion from long-term caring, and it affects many carers physically and emotionally. It is not a sign of not loving the person.

quiz.q: Which helps share the load?
options: A family meeting dividing tasks, including remote ones
quiz.why: A family meeting that divides tasks, including remote ones, shares the load so care is sustainable. Doing everything alone or hiding the problem leads to burnout.

quiz.q: Respite means…
quiz.why: Respite means planned breaks for the carer, and regular rest prevents burnout. It is not a medicine or hospital bill.

quiz.q: If a carer feels hopeless or at risk of harming themselves, call…
quiz.why: A carer who feels hopeless or at risk of self-harm should call 14416 (Tele-MANAS) or 112 for immediate support. 1906 and 1915 are not for this.

lessons.title: Understanding grief

scenes.text: When Jessica’s grandmother dies in Shillong, Jessica, 24, cries at the funeral — then feels strangely numb for weeks.
Months later, hearing Nani’s favourite song in a shop makes her break down. She wonders if she’s ‘doing grief wrong’.
A counsellor explains that grief comes in waves, not neat stages, and that there’s no ‘right’ timeline.
On Nani’s first death anniversary, the family shares stories and cooks her recipes. Jessica feels sad — and close to her.

steps.title: Grief is a natural response to loss
steps.body:
Grief follows the death of a loved one, but also other losses: a pet, a relationship, a job, health, a home. It can affect:
- **Feelings**: sadness, numbness, anger, guilt, relief, anxiety, longing
- **Body**: tiredness, sleep and appetite changes, aches
- **Thinking**: poor concentration, forgetfulness, replaying events
- **Behaviour**: withdrawing, restlessness, visiting or avoiding reminders
All of these can be normal.

steps.title: No fixed stages, no fixed timeline
steps.body: The well-known ‘five stages’ (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance) were first described for dying patients and are **not** a fixed sequence everyone follows. Many people move **back and forth** between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life — this ‘oscillation’ is healthy. Grief often comes in **waves**, triggered by anniversaries, festivals, songs or places. Over time, the waves usually become less frequent and less overwhelming, and people find ways to carry the bond with the person who died.

steps.title: What helps
steps.body:
- Let feelings come; crying is not weakness.
- Keep basic routines: sleep, meals, a short walk.
- **Rituals** — religious or personal — help many people: prayers, lighting a lamp, sharing memories, a memory box, writing a letter.
- Talk to people who listen; share stories of the person.
- Postpone major decisions (selling a house, moving) if you can.
- Be gentle on anniversaries and festivals; plan how you want to spend them.

steps.title: When to seek professional help
steps.body: Consider seeing a doctor, psychologist or counsellor if intense grief seriously disrupts daily life for many months (clinicians assess **prolonged grief** when this continues well beyond the usual time, often around 6–12 months), if you can’t function at work or home, if you are using alcohol or drugs to cope, or if you feel life is not worth living. If you have thoughts of suicide, reach out now: **Tele-MANAS 14416** or **112**. This is general education, not medical advice.

steps.title: Across cultures
steps.body: Every culture has its own ways of mourning — from the 13-day rituals in many Hindu families and the Muslim ‘three days’ of mourning, to Christian memorial services, Sikh Antim Ardas, and Mexico’s Día de Muertos. These traditions give structure, community and meaning. You can honour tradition and also grieve in your own way.

activity.prompt: Think of a loss you’ve experienced. What helped you even a little? What do you wish someone had said or done?
activity.hint: There are no right answers. If writing brings up strong pain, pause and talk to someone you trust.

quiz.q: The ‘five stages of grief’ are…
options: A description that many people don’t follow in order
quiz.why: The 'five stages of grief' are a description that many people do not follow in order, because grief is not linear. They are not a fixed sequence, a legal rule or only for children.

quiz.q: Grief can cause…
options: Emotional, physical, thinking and behaviour changes
quiz.why: Grief can cause emotional, physical, thinking and behaviour changes, because it affects the whole person. It is not only sadness or anger.

quiz.q: Which is generally helpful while grieving?
options: Keeping basic routines and sharing memories
quiz.why: Keeping basic routines and sharing memories supports coping through connection. Pretending nothing happened, isolating or making big decisions immediately is less helpful.

quiz.q: When should a grieving person seek professional help?
options: If grief severely disrupts life for many months or there are thoughts of suicide
quiz.why: Seek professional help if grief severely disrupts life for many months or there are thoughts of suicide. Prolonged or risky grief needs support.

sources: Stroebe & Schut — Dual Process Model of grief

lessons.title: Supporting grieving adults and children — and practical steps after a death

scenes.text: Seven-year-old Arjun’s father dies suddenly in Vadodara. Relatives tell him ‘Papa has gone to sleep’ and ‘Papa is on a long trip’.
Arjun becomes afraid to sleep and keeps asking when Papa will come back.
A child counsellor helps his mother explain gently: ‘Papa died. His body stopped working and he can’t come back. It’s not your fault. We will always remember him.’
Arjun makes a memory book with his mother. He still feels sad, but he sleeps again and asks fewer frightened questions.

steps.title: What to say (and not say) to grieving adults
steps.body:
**Helpful**: ‘I’m so sorry.’ · ‘I’m here for you.’ · ‘I remember when he…’ · ‘You don’t have to talk; I’ll sit with you.’ · Saying the person’s name.
**Unhelpful**: ‘Everything happens for a reason.’ · ‘At least she lived a long life.’ · ‘Be strong.’ · ‘I know exactly how you feel.’ · Changing the subject or avoiding them.
**Practical help beats general offers**: instead of ‘Call me if you need anything’, try ‘I’ll bring dinner on Thursday’ or ‘I can pick up the children from school this week.’ Check in again after weeks and months — support often fades just when loneliness grows.

steps.title: Children grieve differently
steps.body:
- Use **clear, simple words**: ‘died’ and ‘dead’. Phrases like ‘went to sleep’ or ‘we lost him’ can confuse and frighten young children.
- Children under about 5–6 may not understand that death is permanent; they may ask the same questions repeatedly. Answer patiently.
- Children often grieve in **bursts** — crying one moment, playing the next. That’s normal.
- Reassure them: **it’s not their fault**, and who will take care of them.
- Offer choices about attending rituals, explaining what will happen.
- Keep routines; inform teachers.
- Watch for lasting changes (sleep, school, withdrawal, aggression); seek a child counsellor if they persist.

steps.title: Practical steps after a death in India
steps.body:
- **Death registration**: under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act 1969, a death should be reported to the local registrar (municipal/panchayat office) within **21 days**; hospitals usually report deaths that occur there. Get several copies of the **death certificate**.
- Inform banks, insurers, employer/EPFO, pension office; claims are usually made by **nominees** with the death certificate and ID.
- Check for a **will**; legal heirs may need a legal-heir or succession certificate for some assets.
- Close or transfer mobile numbers, email and social media accounts carefully (many platforms offer memorialisation).
- Ask a trusted relative or professional to help — grief makes paperwork harder.
This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Look after yourself too
steps.body: Supporting someone who is grieving can stir your own losses. Take breaks, talk to someone, and remember you don’t have to fix their pain — being present is enough.

activity.prompt: Helpful or unhelpful thing to say to a grieving friend?

items.text: ‘At least he’s in a better place, so don’t cry.’
‘I remember how she always laughed at my jokes.’

quiz.q: Best words for telling a young child about a death?
options: ‘He died. His body stopped working and he can’t come back.’
quiz.why: Use clear words like 'He died. His body stopped working and he can't come back.' Euphemisms such as sleeping or a long trip confuse and frighten young children.

quiz.q: Which offer of support is most useful?
options: ‘I’ll pick up the kids from school this week.’
quiz.why: Specific practical help like 'I'll pick up the kids from school this week' is easier to accept than a vague offer. Avoiding or changing the subject leaves them alone.

quiz.q: A death should generally be registered within…
quiz.why: A death should generally be registered within 21 days under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act 1969. It should not be left for months.

quiz.q: Children grieving in ‘bursts’ — crying then playing — is…
quiz.why: Children often grieve in bursts, crying and then playing, which is normal. It does not mean they do not care.

sources: Registration of Births and Deaths Act 1969
Child bereavement guidance (UNICEF, child psychology literature)

questions.why: Elderline, the national helpline for senior citizens, is 14567. 101 is fire, 1930 is cyber fraud and 1098 is Childline.

questions.q: A non-slip bathroom mat helps prevent…
questions.why: A non-slip bathroom mat helps prevent falls, which are common in bathrooms. It does not stop fever, floods or fraud.

questions.q: Is there one right way to grieve?
questions.why: No, there is no single right way to grieve, because grief varies widely between people.
Signs of caregiver burnout include constant exhaustion and irritability. More energy and better sleep are the opposite.

questions.q: Which phrase is unhelpful to a grieving person?
questions.why: 'Everything happens for a reason' minimises the person's pain, so it is unhelpful. Being present, sharing a kind memory or sitting quietly helps.

questions.q: The 2007 Act lets parents claim maintenance through…
questions.why: Under the 2007 Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, parents claim maintenance through Maintenance Tribunals. The Election Commission, Consumer Commission and RTI are unrelated.

questions.q: Why keep one updated medicine list?
options: Doctors can check doses and interactions
questions.why: One updated medicine list lets doctors check doses and interactions, which prevents errors. It is not decoration or required for voting.

options: Grief only happens near the sea
Feelings rise and fall, often triggered by reminders
questions.why: 'Grief comes in waves' means feelings rise and fall, often triggered by reminders. It does not end in a week or stay unchanged.

questions.q: Telling a 5-year-old ‘Grandpa went to sleep’ may…
questions.why: Telling a 5-year-old 'Grandpa went to sleep' may make them afraid of sleeping, because euphemisms confuse young children. Plain, simple words are better.

questions.q: An elder repeatedly gets lost in a familiar market and forgets bill payments. Best step?
options: Arrange a medical assessment; some causes are treatable
questions.why: Repeatedly getting lost and forgetting bills calls for a medical assessment, because some causes are treatable and early assessment helps. Scolding, ignoring it or removing all freedom is not helpful.

questions.q: Siblings abroad want to help with a parent’s care. Useful remote tasks?
options: Paying for attendants, managing bills, booking appointments, regular video calls, planning respite
questions.why: Distance doesn't prevent sharing the load: siblings abroad can pay for attendants, manage bills, book appointments, hold regular video calls and plan respite. Only sending advice or visiting once a decade does not.

questions.q: Which statement about the ‘five stages’ is accurate?
options: They were described for dying patients and are not a fixed sequence for all grievers
Everyone goes through them in order
questions.why: The five stages were described for dying patients and are not a fixed sequence for all grievers, since modern models emphasise moving back and forth. They do not last exactly a year.

questions.q: Eighteen months after a death, a person still can’t work, avoids everything, and says life feels pointless. Best response?
options: Encourage professional help (possible prolonged grief or depression) and share 14416; call 112 if at immediate risk
questions.why: Eighteen months on, being unable to work, avoiding everything and feeling life is pointless suggests prolonged grief or depression. Encourage professional help and share 14416, and call 112 if at immediate risk.

questions.q: Best combined plan for a carer at risk of burnout?
options: Task list → family meeting to divide work → paid help/day-care where possible → scheduled respite → daily small resets → counselling if low mood persists
questions.why: A sustainable plan shares the load: list tasks, hold a family meeting to divide work, add paid help or day-care, schedule respite, take daily small resets and get counselling if low mood persists. Quitting suddenly or pushing through alone leads to breakdown.

life-safety-firstaid.title: Safety & first aid
life-safety-firstaid.description: Call 112, do CPR, help someone choking, stop bleeding, cool a burn, handle snakebites and dog bites, survive fire, earthquake and flood, and stay safe on Indian roads.

courses.title: First aid that saves lives
courses.summary: The first minutes matter most. Learn to check safety and call 112, give CPR, clear choking, control bleeding, cool burns, and handle snakebites, dog bites and heatstroke — with myths busted.
outcomes: Learners can follow Danger–Response–Send for help–Airway–Breathing–CPR
Learners can give hands-only CPR at the right rate and depth
Learners can help a choking adult, child and infant
Learners can control bleeding and cool a burn correctly
Learners can explain snakebite do’s and don’ts and rabies prevention

lessons.title: The first minute: check, call 112, act

scenes.text: At a bus stop in Bhubaneswar, an elderly man suddenly falls. A crowd forms but everyone just watches.
Sixteen-year-old Ritika, who learned first aid at school, checks for traffic, taps his shoulders and shouts, ‘Uncle, can you hear me?’
She points at a man: ‘You in the blue shirt — call 112, tell them a man is unconscious at the Rasulgarh bus stop.’
She checks his breathing. He is breathing normally, so she turns him into the recovery position and stays with him until the ambulance arrives.

steps.title: D-R-S-A-B-C: the order that keeps everyone safe
steps.body:
- **D — Danger**: check for traffic, fire, electricity, gas, falling objects. Don’t become a second victim.
- **R — Response**: tap the shoulders and shout. Do they answer or move?
- **S — Send for help**: call **112** (India’s single emergency number) or ask a specific person to call. Put the phone on speaker.
- **A — Airway**: tilt the head back gently and lift the chin.
- **B — Breathing**: look, listen and feel for **normal** breathing for up to 10 seconds. Occasional gasps are **not** normal breathing.
- **C — CPR**: if not breathing normally, start chest compressions (next lesson) and send for an AED (defibrillator) if one is nearby.

steps.title: Calling 112 well
steps.body:
112 connects to police, fire and ambulance services (108 or 102 also work for ambulances in many states). Say clearly:
1. **Where** you are (landmark, road, pin location — share live location if possible)
2. **What** happened
3. **How many** people hurt and their condition (conscious? breathing?)
4. Your phone number
Don’t hang up until told; they may guide you. Many phones also have an SOS shortcut (for example pressing the power button several times).

steps.title: The recovery position
steps.body:
For someone **unconscious but breathing normally** (and no suspected spine injury):
1. Kneel beside them; place the near arm at a right angle.
2. Bring the far arm across the chest, back of hand against their near cheek.
3. Bend the far knee up; pull on that knee to roll them towards you onto their side.
4. Tilt the head back to keep the airway open; mouth pointing slightly down so fluids drain.
5. Keep checking breathing until help arrives. If breathing stops, roll them back and start CPR.

steps.title: Myths that cause harm
steps.body:
- Don’t pour water into an unconscious person’s mouth — they can choke.
- Don’t make a fainted person sit up quickly or crowd them.
- Onion or shoe smelling doesn’t treat fits (seizures). For a seizure: clear the space, cushion the head, **don’t restrain and don’t put anything in the mouth**, time it, recovery position after; call 112 if it lasts more than 5 minutes, repeats, or it’s their first.
- A crowd watching is not help. **Point at one person** and give one task.

steps.title: Learn hands-on
steps.body: This course is general education, not a substitute for a certified first-aid course. Organisations like the Indian Red Cross Society and St John Ambulance run practical trainings — doing it once with a manikin makes you far more confident.

activity.prompt: Put the first-aid check in the right order.
items: Check for danger to yourself and others
Check response: tap shoulders and shout
Open the airway: head tilt, chin lift
Check for normal breathing (up to 10 seconds)
If not breathing normally, start CPR

quiz.q: India’s single emergency number is…
quiz.why: India's single emergency number is 112, which connects police, fire and ambulance. 1098 is Childline, 1930 is cyber fraud and 100 is police only.

quiz.q: Why check for danger first?
options: To avoid becoming a second victim
quiz.why: Check for danger first so you don't become a second victim, since an injured helper can't help anyone.

quiz.q: An unconscious person is breathing normally. You should…
options: Place them in the recovery position and monitor
quiz.why: An unconscious person who is breathing normally should be placed in the recovery position and monitored, which keeps the airway open. CPR is only for no normal breathing, and water risks choking.

quiz.q: During a seizure you should…
options: Put a spoon in their mouth
Clear space, cushion the head, time it
quiz.why: During a seizure, clear space, cushion the head and time it, to protect from injury. Never restrain the person or put anything in the mouth.

quiz.q: Occasional gasps in an unresponsive person mean…
quiz.why: Occasional gasps in an unresponsive person are agonal breathing, a sign of cardiac arrest, not normal breathing. Start CPR and call for help.

sources: Indian Red Cross Society first aid manual
International first aid & resuscitation guidelines (IFRC, ILCOR)

scenes.text: At a Sunday match in Ludhiana, 52-year-old Mr. Gill collapses on the pitch. He doesn’t respond and is only gasping.
His nephew Harpreet calls 112 on speaker and starts pressing hard on the centre of his chest, counting aloud.
Someone remembers a song with the right beat. Two others take turns every two minutes.
The ambulance team uses a defibrillator. Mr. Gill survives. Doctors say the early CPR kept his brain alive.

steps.title: Why CPR works
steps.body: In **cardiac arrest** the heart stops pumping effectively. Without blood flow, brain damage begins within minutes. **CPR** (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) pushes blood to the brain and heart by squeezing the heart between the breastbone and spine. It buys time until a **defibrillator (AED)** and the ambulance arrive. Without CPR, the chance of survival falls rapidly with every minute.

steps.title: Hands-only CPR for an adult
steps.body:
1. Person on their back on a firm surface.
2. Heel of one hand on the **centre of the chest** (lower half of the breastbone), other hand on top, fingers interlocked.
3. Arms straight, shoulders over hands.
4. Press down **5–6 cm** and let the chest **fully come back up** each time.
5. Rate: **100–120 compressions per minute** (about two per second).
6. Don’t stop except to let an AED analyse, or if they start breathing normally, or professionals take over.
7. Swap with another helper about **every 2 minutes** — quality drops when you tire.

steps.title: Rescue breaths and AEDs
steps.body:
If you are **trained and willing**, give **30 compressions then 2 rescue breaths** (head tilt, chin lift, pinch nose, seal mouth, breathe until the chest rises, about 1 second each). If not trained or unwilling, **hands-only CPR** is far better than nothing.

**AED**: switch it on and follow the voice prompts; stick pads as shown on the pictures; make sure nobody touches the person when it says ‘analysing’ or ‘shock’. AEDs are designed for untrained people and won’t shock if it isn’t needed.

steps.title: Children and infants (if you know how)
steps.body:
- **Child** (about 1 year to puberty): one or two hands, press about **5 cm** (one-third of chest depth). Many guidelines suggest 5 initial rescue breaths if trained, then 30:2.
- **Infant** (under 1): two fingers (or two thumbs encircling) on the centre of the chest just below the nipple line, press about **4 cm** (one-third of chest depth), 100–120 per minute.
In children, arrest is often due to breathing problems, so rescue breaths matter more — another reason to take a hands-on course.

steps.title: Fears that stop people
steps.body:
- **‘I might break a rib.’** It can happen; a broken rib heals, death doesn’t.
- **‘I might be blamed.’** India’s Good Samaritan protections (Motor Vehicles Act section 134A and Supreme Court-approved guidelines) protect people who help in good faith in road emergencies, and courts generally respect good-faith rescue.
- **Pressing too gently or too slowly** is the most common mistake. Push hard and fast. Use the **CPR rhythm** lab to practise the beat.

statements.s: Adult CPR compressions should be 100–120 per minute.
statements.why: About two compressions per second.

statements.s: You should press about 1 cm deep on an adult’s chest.
statements.why: Adults need 5–6 cm to move blood.

statements.s: Hands-only CPR is useful even if you can’t give rescue breaths.
statements.why: Compressions alone circulate blood in the first minutes.

statements.s: An AED will shock anyone it is attached to, even if not needed.
statements.why: AEDs analyse the heart rhythm and only advise a shock when appropriate.

statements.s: Let the chest fully rise between compressions.
statements.why: Full recoil lets the heart refill with blood.

quiz.q: Where do you place your hands for adult CPR?
options: Centre of the chest, lower half of the breastbone
quiz.why: For adult CPR, place your hands on the centre of the chest, on the lower half of the breastbone, where compressions squeeze the heart.

quiz.q: How deep for an adult?
quiz.why: The recommended depth for adult chest compressions is 5–6 cm, which is enough to pump blood. Just touching or 1–2 cm is too shallow, and 10–12 cm is too deep.

quiz.q: If trained, the compression-to-breath ratio for adults is…
quiz.why: If trained, the adult ratio is 30 compressions then 2 breaths, which is 30:2.

quiz.q: Why swap rescuers every 2 minutes?
quiz.why: Rescuers swap every 2 minutes because compression quality drops with fatigue; tired rescuers press too shallow or slow.

quiz.q: When should you stop CPR?
options: When the person breathes normally, professionals take over, or the AED tells you to pause
quiz.why: Continue CPR until the person breathes normally, professionals take over or the AED tells you to pause, or until you are physically unable. A ringing phone or a crowd are not reasons to stop.

lessons.title: Choking: adults, children and babies

scenes.text: At a wedding lunch in Udaipur, Mr. Rathore suddenly clutches his throat. He can’t speak or cough.
A caterer, Maria, trained in first aid, asks, ‘Are you choking?’ He nods.
She leans him forward and gives firm back blows. Nothing. She switches to abdominal thrusts — on the third, a piece of food flies out.
She still advises him to see a doctor, because abdominal thrusts can cause internal injury.

steps.title: Mild vs severe choking
steps.body:
- **Mild**: the person can **cough, speak or breathe**. Encourage them to keep coughing hard. Don’t slap their back or give water yet. Stay with them.
- **Severe**: they **can’t speak, cough effectively or breathe**, may clutch the throat, go silent, turn blue. Act immediately and call 112 (or get someone to call).

steps.title: Adult or child over 1 year: back blows and abdominal thrusts
steps.body:
1. Stand slightly behind, support the chest with one hand, **lean them forward**.
2. Give up to **5 sharp back blows** between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. Check after each.
3. If still choking: stand behind, wrap arms round their waist, make a fist just **above the navel** (below the ribs), grab it with the other hand, pull sharply **inwards and upwards** — up to **5 abdominal thrusts**.
4. Repeat 5 back blows and 5 thrusts until the object comes out or they become unresponsive.
5. If they become **unresponsive**: lower them to the floor, call 112, start **CPR**. Check the mouth for a visible object before breaths; never do blind finger sweeps.

steps.title: Babies under 1 year
steps.body:
**No abdominal thrusts for infants.**
1. Lay the baby **face down along your forearm**, head lower than chest, supporting the jaw.
2. Give up to **5 back blows** between the shoulder blades.
3. Turn the baby face up along your other arm; give up to **5 chest thrusts** with two fingers on the centre of the chest just below the nipple line.
4. Repeat until cleared or the baby becomes unresponsive — then start infant CPR and call 112.

steps.title: Special cases and after-care
steps.body:
- **Pregnant** or very large person: give **chest thrusts** (hands on the centre of the chest) instead of abdominal thrusts.
- **Alone and choking**: call 112, then press your upper abdomen hard against a chair back or table edge.
- After any abdominal thrusts, the person should be **checked by a doctor**.
- Prevention for small children: cut grapes and similar round foods lengthwise, avoid whole nuts and hard sweets for toddlers, supervise eating, keep coins, button batteries and small toy parts out of reach. **Button batteries** swallowed are an emergency — go to hospital immediately.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving water to a severely choking person.
- Turning a baby upside down by the legs and shaking.
- Blind finger sweeps that push the object deeper.
- Thrusts on someone who is coughing well (let them cough).

a.text: Your friend at dinner grabs her throat. You ask ‘Are you choking?’ She is coughing loudly and can speak a word.

choices.label: Encourage her to keep coughing and stay with her
choices.feedback: Correct — effective coughing is the best way to clear it.

choices.label: Immediately give abdominal thrusts
choices.feedback: Not yet — thrusts are for severe choking when coughing fails.

b.text: Now she can’t make any sound and her lips are turning blue.

choices.label: Lean her forward and give up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts; get someone to call 112
choices.feedback: Exactly right.

choices.label: Give her a glass of water
choices.feedback: Water can’t pass and may worsen things.

c.text: After the second thrust the food pops out and she breathes. What next?

choices.label: Advise a medical check-up because thrusts can cause internal injury
choices.feedback: Yes — always get checked after abdominal thrusts.

choices.label: Continue dinner, nothing else needed
choices.feedback: She’s breathing, but she should still see a doctor.

bad.text: She collapses. Lower her to the floor, call 112 and begin CPR, checking the mouth for a visible object before any breaths.

good.text: She’s safe. You recognised mild vs severe choking and acted in the right order.

quiz.q: A choking adult is coughing forcefully. You should…
quiz.why: A choking adult who is coughing forcefully has a mild blockage, so encourage coughing and watch closely, since coughing works best. Abdominal thrusts are for when they cannot cough or breathe.

quiz.q: For a choking baby under 1, you should NOT give…
quiz.why: Do not give abdominal thrusts to a choking baby under 1, as they can injure the infant's organs. Use back blows and chest thrusts and call 112.

quiz.q: Where do you position your fist for abdominal thrusts?
options: Just above the navel, below the ribs
quiz.why: For abdominal thrusts, place your fist just above the navel and below the ribs, which pushes air upward from the lungs. The ribs or neck would not work and could injure.

quiz.q: A pregnant woman is severely choking. Use…
quiz.why: For a severely choking pregnant woman use chest thrusts, which avoid pressure on the abdomen. Water or doing nothing is unsafe.

quiz.q: Swallowed button battery in a child means…
quiz.why: A swallowed button battery needs hospital immediately, because it can burn through tissue within hours. Waiting, milk or vomiting is dangerous.

sources: ILCOR / Resuscitation Council guidance on foreign body airway obstruction
Indian Academy of Pediatrics child safety advice

scenes.text: In Kozhikode, 14-year-old Aysha’s mother slices her palm deeply while cutting jackfruit. Blood is everywhere.
Aysha presses a clean towel hard on the wound and holds the hand up, while her brother calls 112.
A week later her little cousin touches a hot tawa. Grandma reaches for toothpaste — Aysha says, ‘No! Cool water for 20 minutes.’
The doctor later tells them both actions prevented much worse injuries.

steps.title: Severe bleeding: press, don’t peek
steps.body:
1. Protect yourself (gloves or a plastic bag if available).
2. Press **firmly and directly** on the wound with a clean cloth or pad. **Keep pressure** for at least 10 minutes without lifting to check.
3. If blood soaks through, **add more cloth on top** — don’t remove the first layer.
4. Help them lie down if they feel faint; keep them warm.
5. Call 112 for heavy bleeding.
6. If an object is stuck in the wound, **don’t pull it out** — press around it.
Trained responders may use a **tourniquet** for life-threatening limb bleeding that pressure can’t control; note the time it was applied.

steps.title: Nosebleeds and small cuts
steps.body:
**Nosebleed**: sit up, **lean forward** (not back), pinch the soft part of the nose for 10–15 minutes, breathe through the mouth. Tilting the head back makes blood go down the throat. See a doctor if it lasts beyond 20 minutes, follows a head injury, or happens often.

**Small cuts**: rinse with clean running water, gentle pressure, cover with a clean dressing. Watch for infection signs (spreading redness, swelling, pus, fever). Ask a doctor about tetanus protection for dirty or deep wounds.

steps.title: Burns: cool, cover, call
steps.body:
1. **Cool** the burn under cool (not icy) **running water for 20 minutes**, as soon as possible.
2. Remove rings, watches and clothing near the burn unless stuck to the skin.
3. **Cover** loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy cloth.
4. Keep the person warm (cool the burn, not the whole body).
5. **Get medical help** for: burns larger than the person’s palm, any burn on face, hands, feet, genitals or joints, deep burns (white, charred, painless), electrical and chemical burns, and burns in babies, children and older adults.
**Chemical burns**: brush off dry powder, then rinse with plenty of running water for at least 20 minutes.

steps.title: Burn myths
steps.body: **Never** put ice, butter, ghee, oil, toothpaste, turmeric paste, egg white or ink on a burn. They trap heat, cause infection or damage tissue. **Don’t pop blisters** — they protect the skin underneath.

steps.title: Suspected broken bones and head injuries
steps.body:
- **Fracture signs**: pain, swelling, deformity, can’t move or bear weight. **Don’t try to straighten it.** Support it in the position found (padding, sling, rolled newspaper splint if trained); apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth; get medical help.
- **Possible neck/spine injury** (fall from height, road crash, diving): don’t move them unless in danger; keep head and neck still; call 112.
- **Head injury danger signs** — get urgent help: unconsciousness even briefly, repeated vomiting, worsening headache, confusion, drowsiness, fits, clear fluid from nose or ears, weakness on one side, unequal pupils.
This is general education, not medical advice.

activity.prompt: Do or don’t? Sort these first-aid actions.

items.text: Cool a burn under running water for 20 minutes
Press hard on a bleeding wound with a clean cloth
Lift the cloth every minute to check the bleeding
Lean forward and pinch the nose for a nosebleed
Pull out a knife stuck in a wound

quiz.q: How long should you cool a burn under running water?
quiz.why: Cool a burn under running water for about 20 minutes, which limits damage. Ten seconds is too short, and ice or leaving it can worsen the injury.

quiz.q: Blood soaks through the cloth. You…
options: Add more cloth on top and keep pressing
quiz.why: If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top and keep pressing, since removing the first layer disturbs clotting. Stopping pressure or pouring water won't control bleeding.

quiz.q: For a nosebleed, the person should…
options: Lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose
quiz.why: For a nosebleed, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose, which stops blood going down the throat. Tilting back or lying flat lets blood be swallowed or inhaled.

quiz.q: Which burn always needs medical help?
options: A tiny sunburn on the arm
Any burn on a baby’s face
quiz.why: Any burn on a baby's face needs medical help, because face burns and burns in infants need professional care. A tiny sunburn or a warm cup touch is minor.

quiz.q: Which is a head-injury danger sign?
quiz.why: Repeated vomiting after a head injury is a danger sign because it can mean brain injury, so seek urgent care. A mild bruise, sneezing or hunger are not warning signs.

lessons.title: Snakebite, dog bite and heatstroke: myths vs facts

scenes.text: In a village near Nashik, farmer Sanjay is bitten on the ankle while walking through a field at night.
Neighbours want to tie a tight rope, cut the wound and take him to a local healer.
His daughter Pallavi, a nursing student, says: ‘No cutting, no sucking, no healer. Keep his leg still and get him to the government hospital now.’
At the hospital he receives antivenom in time. The doctor says the hours saved made the difference.

steps.title: Snakebite in India: the facts
steps.body: India has among the highest numbers of snakebite deaths in the world — tens of thousands each year, mostly farmers, rural families and children. Most deaths are caused by the **‘Big Four’**: **Indian cobra, common krait, Russell’s viper and saw-scaled viper**. Many bites are from non-venomous snakes or are ‘dry’ bites, but you **can’t tell safely**, so treat every bite as an emergency. **Antivenom** is the only proven treatment and is available in many government hospitals.

steps.title: What to DO
steps.body:
1. Move away from the snake; don’t try to catch or kill it (a photo from a safe distance can help, but don’t waste time).
2. **Keep calm and still**; panic and movement can speed the spread of venom.
3. **Immobilise** the bitten limb like a fracture (splint, sling), keep it roughly at heart level.
4. Remove rings, bangles, anklets, watches and tight clothing (swelling comes fast).
5. **Go to the nearest hospital with antivenom immediately** — call 112 or 108; carry the person if possible rather than letting them walk.
6. Note the time of the bite and symptoms (drooping eyelids, difficulty breathing or swallowing, bleeding gums, swelling).

steps.title: What NOT to do (common myths)
steps.body:
- ❌ **Cutting** the wound or **sucking** out venom — causes infection and bleeding; doesn’t remove venom.
- ❌ **Tight tourniquets** or ropes — can cause severe tissue damage and loss of the limb.
- ❌ Ice, electric shock, chemicals, herbs, ‘snake stones’, alcohol.
- ❌ Waiting for a faith healer or ‘mantra’ treatment — the lost time is the most dangerous mistake.
- ❌ Assuming no pain means no danger: **krait bites** often happen at night to people sleeping on the floor and may be painless, yet deadly.
**Prevention**: sleep on a raised bed under a tucked-in mosquito net, carry a torch at night, wear boots in fields, clear rubbish and rat-attracting grain stores near homes.

steps.title: Dog and animal bites: rabies is preventable
steps.body:
Rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms start — but **completely preventable** with prompt care.
1. **Immediately wash the wound with soap and running water for about 15 minutes.**
2. Apply an antiseptic (such as povidone-iodine) if available.
3. **Go to a hospital the same day** for anti-rabies vaccine, and rabies immunoglobulin if the doctor advises (for deeper bites/scratches). Government hospitals provide these.
4. Complete **every dose** of the schedule.
This applies to bites or scratches from dogs, cats, monkeys and other mammals. Don’t apply chilli, turmeric or oil, and don’t wait to ‘watch the dog’ before starting treatment.

steps.title: Heat exhaustion and heatstroke
steps.body:
**Heat exhaustion**: heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea. Move to shade, loosen clothes, sip water or **ORS**, cool with wet cloths.
**Heatstroke** is an emergency: very high body temperature, confusion, slurred speech, fainting or fits, skin may be hot (dry or sweaty). **Call 112**, cool the person rapidly (water on skin, fan, wet sheets, ice packs at neck, armpits, groin), don’t give drinks if they are confused or unconscious.
Prevention in summer: drink water regularly, avoid strenuous work at midday, wear light loose cotton, cover the head, check on elderly neighbours and never leave children or pets in parked vehicles.

statements.s: Sucking out venom is an effective snakebite treatment.
statements.why: It doesn’t remove venom and can cause infection.

statements.s: Antivenom given in a hospital is the proven treatment for venomous snakebite.
statements.why: Speed to hospital is the most important action.

statements.s: Krait bites can be painless but deadly, often during sleep at night.
statements.why: That’s why sleeping under a net on a raised bed helps.

statements.s: After a dog bite, washing the wound with soap and water for 15 minutes reduces rabies risk.
statements.why: It’s the crucial first step, followed by vaccination.

statements.s: A tight rope above a snakebite is recommended.
statements.why: Tight tourniquets can cause limb damage and are not recommended.

statements.s: A confused, very hot person in summer may have heatstroke — a medical emergency.
statements.why: Call 112 and cool them rapidly.

quiz.q: First thing to do after a snakebite (once away from the snake)?
options: Keep still, immobilise the limb and go to hospital
quiz.why: After a snakebite, keep still, immobilise the limb and go to hospital, because time to antivenom saves lives. Cutting, alcohol or visiting a healer wastes time.

quiz.q: Which is one of India’s ‘Big Four’ venomous snakes?
quiz.why: Russell's viper is one of India's 'Big Four' venomous snakes, with the cobra, krait and saw-scaled viper. Pythons, sand boas and rat snakes are not among them.

quiz.q: After a dog bite you should…
options: Wait 10 days to see if the dog gets sick
Wash with soap and water ~15 minutes and get anti-rabies vaccination the same day
quiz.why: After a dog bite wash with soap and water for about 15 minutes and get anti-rabies vaccination the same day. Waiting 10 days or doing nothing for a scratch risks rabies.

quiz.q: Why remove bangles after a bite on the arm?
options: Swelling can make them cut off circulation
quiz.why: Remove bangles after a bite on the arm because rapid swelling can make them cut off circulation. It is not about snakes or fashion.

quiz.q: Best drink for someone with mild heat exhaustion who is alert?
quiz.why: A person with mild heat exhaustion who is alert should rehydrate gently with sips of water or ORS. Alcohol and very hot tea do not help, and nothing at all risks worsening dehydration.

sources: National guidelines for management of snakebite (MoHFW)

questions.why: India's all-emergency number is 112, which connects all emergency services. 1930 is cyber fraud and 1906 is LPG.

questions.q: A burn should be cooled with…
questions.why: Cool a burn with cool running water for about 20 minutes. Ice, toothpaste or butter can worsen the damage.
For a nosebleed, lean forward so blood does not run down the throat. Leaning back, lying down or hanging upside down is wrong.
Adult CPR should be done at 100–120 compressions per minute, about two per second.

options: Up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts
questions.why: For a severely choking adult, give up to 5 back blows then up to 5 abdominal thrusts, alternating. Water or CPR while they are still conscious and standing is wrong.
After a snakebite, immobilise the limb and rush to hospital, because immobilisation and antivenom are key. Cutting, sucking, ice and tight tourniquets cause harm.

questions.q: An unconscious person is breathing normally. Next?
questions.why: If an unconscious person is breathing normally, use the recovery position and monitor, which keeps the airway open. CPR is for those not breathing normally, and sitting up or food is unsafe.

options: 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts, repeated
questions.why: For a choking infant, give 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts, repeated. No abdominal thrusts, blind finger sweeps or shaking.
Adult compressions should be 5–6 cm deep, enough to pump blood. Too shallow is ineffective and too deep can injure.

questions.q: Someone collapses from a live electric wire. First?
options: Switch off power or separate with a dry non-conductor, then call 112 and check breathing
Start CPR while they touch the wire
questions.why: Danger first: switch off the power or separate the person from the wire with a dry non-conductor, then call 112 and check breathing. Grabbing their hand or pouring water can electrocute you too, and CPR cannot start while they are still in contact.

questions.q: A bite from a street dog left only a small scratch with slight bleeding. Best action?
options: Wash 15 minutes with soap and water and see a doctor the same day for anti-rabies treatment
questions.why: A scratch that breaks the skin can transmit rabies. Wash for 15 minutes with soap and water and see a doctor the same day for anti-rabies treatment; ignoring it, turmeric alone or waiting a month is unsafe.

questions.q: During CPR an AED arrives. You should…
options: Switch it on and follow prompts while minimising pauses in compressions
questions.why: Early defibrillation greatly improves survival, so switch the AED on and follow its prompts while keeping pauses in compressions as short as possible. Waiting for doctors or reading the full manual wastes critical time.

questions.q: A villager bitten at night while sleeping on the floor feels no pain but later has drooping eyelids. Likely and right action?
options: Possible krait envenoming — emergency transport to a hospital with antivenom
questions.why: A painless night bite followed by drooping eyelids suggests krait envenoming, whose neurotoxin causes ptosis and can stop breathing. This is time-critical, so get emergency transport to a hospital with antivenom; a healer, antihistamine or sleep can be fatal.

questions.q: Deep cut on the forearm bleeding heavily; cloth soaked. Best sequence?
options: Add more cloth, keep firm direct pressure, lay person down, call 112; tourniquet only if trained and bleeding is life-threatening
questions.why: Continuous firm direct pressure is the cornerstone of bleeding control: add more cloth on top, keep pressing, lay the person down and call 112. Use a tourniquet only if trained and the bleeding is life-threatening; removing the cloth or applying turmeric disrupts clotting.

courses.title: Fire, earthquake, flood: be ready
courses.summary: What to do before, during and after a fire, earthquake, flood or cyclone, how to use an extinguisher, and how to prepare an emergency kit and family plan.
outcomes: Learners can escape a fire safely and use an extinguisher (PASS)
Learners can act correctly during an earthquake (Drop, Cover, Hold On)
Learners can follow flood and cyclone warnings and stay safe
Learners can prepare an emergency kit and a family communication plan

lessons.title: Fire safety: prevent, escape, extinguish

scenes.text: At 2 am in a Mumbai apartment, 15-year-old Zubin wakes to a beeping smoke alarm and smells burning.
He touches the bedroom door with the back of his hand — it’s cool. He opens it slowly; smoke is near the ceiling.
He wakes his family; they crawl low, take the stairs (not the lift) and meet at the society gate.
They call 101 / 112. A short circuit in a neighbour’s flat had started the fire. Everyone escaped because they had practised.

steps.title: Prevention first
steps.body:
Most home fires start in the kitchen, from electrical faults, or from candles, diyas, mosquito coils, cigarettes and firecrackers.
- Never leave cooking unattended.
- Don’t overload sockets; replace damaged wires; switch off appliances at night.
- Keep diyas and candles away from curtains; don’t let children play with matches.
- Keep balconies and staircases free of clutter; never lock fire exits.
- Install **smoke alarms** and test them monthly.

steps.title: If there is a fire: get out, stay out, call
steps.body:
1. Shout ‘Fire!’ to warn everyone.
2. Before opening a door, feel it with the **back of your hand**. If hot, don’t open — use another way.
3. Smoke kills faster than flames: **crawl low** where air is cleaner; cover nose and mouth with cloth.
4. Use **stairs, never lifts**.
5. Close doors behind you to slow the fire.
6. Once out, **don’t go back in** for belongings.
7. Call **101** (fire) or **112**.
If trapped: close the door, block gaps with wet cloth, go to a window, signal with a cloth or torch, and call 112 with your exact location.

steps.title: Stop, drop and roll
steps.body: If your clothes catch fire: **Stop** (don’t run — running fans flames), **Drop** to the ground, cover your face with your hands, **Roll** over and over until flames are out. Then cool burns with water for 20 minutes. Help another person by wrapping them in a heavy blanket or rug (not synthetic) and rolling them.

steps.title: Using a fire extinguisher: PASS
steps.body:
Only for a **small fire** and only if you have a clear escape route behind you.
- **P**ull the pin.
- **A**im the nozzle at the **base** of the fire (not the flames).
- **S**queeze the handle.
- **S**weep side to side.
A common type is **ABC dry powder**, used on ordinary materials, flammable liquids and electrical fires (after switching power off if possible). **Never use water on electrical or oil fires.** If the fire doesn’t shrink within seconds, leave and call for help.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Draw your home’s escape plan: two ways out of each room, and a meeting point outside. Practise once with your family. Find your building’s extinguisher and check its pressure gauge is in the green.

activity.prompt: Arrange the PASS steps for using an extinguisher.
items: Aim at the base of the fire

quiz.q: During a building fire, which should you use?
options: Window jump from a high floor
quiz.why: Use the stairs in a building fire, because lifts can fail or open onto a fire floor. Jumping from a high floor or waiting in the lift lobby is dangerous.

quiz.q: Why crawl low in smoke?
options: Cleaner, cooler air is near the floor
quiz.why: Crawl low in smoke because smoke and heat rise, so cleaner, cooler air is near the floor. It is about breathing, not rules or speed.

quiz.q: Your clothes catch fire. Do…
quiz.why: If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop and roll to smother the flames. Running or waving your arms feeds the fire with more air.

quiz.q: Aim an extinguisher at…
quiz.why: Aim the extinguisher at the base of the fire, where the fuel is. Aiming at smoke, flame tops or the ceiling does not put it out.

quiz.q: Fire services number in India (also reachable via 112)?
quiz.why: 101 is the fire services number in India, also reachable via 112. 1906 is LPG, 14416 is mental health and 1098 is Childline.

sources: National Building Code of India (fire and life safety)

lessons.title: Earthquakes: Drop, Cover, Hold On

scenes.text: Class 9 students in Guwahati are in maths class when the room begins to shake and the fan swings.
Their teacher, Mr. Bora, calls, ‘Drop, cover, hold on!’ Everyone gets under their desks, holding the legs.
The shaking lasts about 20 seconds. When it stops, they walk out calmly in a line to the open ground, away from buildings.
They wait for aftershocks to pass and for official updates. No one is hurt — they had drilled it twice that year.

steps.title: India’s earthquake risk
steps.body: A large part of India lies in moderate to very high seismic zones — especially the Himalayan belt, the North-East, parts of Gujarat (Kutch) and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands. Earthquakes can’t be predicted precisely, so **preparation** matters. Most injuries are caused by **falling objects and collapsing structures**, not the ground movement itself.

steps.title: During shaking: Drop, Cover, Hold On
steps.body:
- **Drop** onto your hands and knees before the shaking knocks you down.
- **Cover** your head and neck under a sturdy table or desk; if none, crouch next to an interior wall away from windows and cover your head with your arms.
- **Hold on** to your shelter until the shaking stops.
**Indoors**: stay in — don’t run out during shaking (falling debris near exits is deadly); avoid windows, glass, almirahs, hanging objects. Don’t use lifts.
**Outdoors**: move to an open area away from buildings, trees, poles and wires.
**In a vehicle**: stop in an open place, away from bridges and flyovers; stay inside.

steps.title: After the shaking
steps.body:
- Expect **aftershocks**; move carefully to open ground.
- Check yourself and others for injuries; give first aid.
- If you smell gas, don’t use flames or switches; turn off the regulator; leave.
- Avoid damaged buildings; listen to official updates on radio/TV/government apps.
- **If trapped**: cover your mouth with cloth, don’t light a match, tap on a pipe or wall or use a whistle so rescuers can hear; shout only as a last resort (to save energy and avoid inhaling dust).
- Use SMS or messages rather than calls to keep networks free.

steps.title: Prepare your home
steps.body:
- Fix heavy almirahs, bookshelves and water heaters to walls.
- Keep heavy items on low shelves; don’t hang heavy frames over beds.
- Know how to switch off gas and electricity.
- When building or buying, ask whether the structure follows earthquake-resistant codes (BIS codes for seismic design).

steps.title: Myths
steps.body:
- ‘Stand in a doorway’ — in modern homes doorways are not stronger than other parts, and doors swing; Drop, Cover, Hold On is safer.
- ‘Run outside immediately’ — many injuries happen to people running out while debris falls.
- Viral messages predicting the ‘exact date of the next big quake’ are false; earthquakes can’t be predicted that way.

a.text: You’re on the 3rd floor of your home and the building starts shaking strongly.

choices.label: Run to the lift
choices.feedback: Lifts can jam or fail during quakes.

choices.label: Drop, take cover under a sturdy table and hold on
choices.feedback: Correct — protect your head from falling objects.

choices.label: Run down the stairs while it’s shaking
choices.feedback: Stairs are dangerous during shaking; wait until it stops.

b.text: The shaking stops. You smell gas in the kitchen.

choices.label: Switch on the light to check
choices.feedback: A spark could ignite the gas.

choices.label: Don’t touch switches; turn off the regulator if safe, open windows, and leave calmly to open ground
choices.feedback: Well done.

bad.text: That choice increased your risk. Remember: Drop, Cover, Hold On during shaking; avoid lifts and sparks afterwards.

good.text: You’re safe in open ground, away from buildings, waiting for official updates and watching for aftershocks.

quiz.q: During an earthquake indoors you should…
quiz.why: Indoors during an earthquake, Drop, Cover and Hold On, which protects you from falling objects. Running outside, standing by a window or using the lift is dangerous.

quiz.q: Most earthquake injuries are caused by…
quiz.why: Most earthquake injuries come from falling objects and collapsing structures, which is why taking cover is crucial. The ground opening, rain or noise are not the main causes.

quiz.q: If trapped under debris, you should…
options: Tap on a pipe or wall and cover your mouth
quiz.why: If trapped under debris, tap on a pipe or wall and cover your mouth. Tapping helps rescuers find you and saves energy, and covering limits dust; a match could ignite gas, and shouting wastes energy.

quiz.q: Outdoors during shaking, go to…
options: An open area away from buildings, trees and wires
quiz.why: Outdoors during shaking, go to an open area away from buildings, trees and wires, which avoids falling hazards. Walls, shops and flyovers can collapse onto you.

scenes.text: In Kerala’s monsoon, the Joseph family hears a district alert on TV: heavy rain, rivers may overflow.
Anna, 16, packs the emergency bag, puts documents in a waterproof pouch and charges power banks.
Her father wants to drive across a flooded road to reach relatives. Anna reminds him: ‘Just 30 cm of moving water can float a car.’
They go to the relief camp at the school on higher ground instead. Their house floods, but everyone is safe.

steps.title: Understand warnings
steps.body: The **India Meteorological Department (IMD)** issues colour-coded weather warnings: **Green** (no action), **Yellow** (be aware), **Orange** (be prepared), **Red** (take action). State and district disaster management authorities announce evacuations. Follow official channels — TV, radio, official government apps and SMS alerts — and ignore unverified forwards.

steps.title: Before and during a flood
steps.body:
**Before**: move valuables and documents up high; keep the emergency kit ready; know the nearest high ground or relief shelter; switch off the electricity main if water may enter.
**During**:
- **Never walk, swim or drive through flood water.** About 15 cm of fast water can knock an adult down, and around 30 cm can float many cars.
- Stay away from electric poles and fallen wires.
- If trapped in a building, go to the highest floor or roof (not a closed attic), signal for help.
- Drink only boiled, bottled or chlorinated water.

steps.title: Cyclones
steps.body: India’s east coast (Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu) and west coast (Gujarat, Maharashtra) face cyclones. **Before landfall**: follow evacuation orders, secure loose items, stock water and food, charge phones, store documents safely. **During**: stay indoors away from windows. The **‘eye’** may bring a sudden calm — **don’t go out**; winds return from the other direction. **After**: avoid fallen wires and damaged structures; wait for the official all-clear. Odisha’s strong early warning and evacuation system has greatly reduced cyclone deaths compared with the 1999 super cyclone — preparation works.

steps.title: After the water goes down
steps.body:
- Don’t switch on electricity until checked by an electrician.
- Watch for snakes and insects in homes.
- Throw away food that touched flood water.
- Disinfect water and surfaces; watch for diarrhoea, fever, leptospirosis (rat urine in flood water — seek a doctor if fever follows wading), dengue and malaria.
- Photograph damage for insurance and government relief claims.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Find the nearest relief shelter or high ground for your home. Save your district disaster control room number. Identify the weather-alert source you’ll trust.

activity.prompt: Match the IMD warning colour to the action.

quiz.q: How much fast-flowing water can float many cars?
quiz.why: About 30 cm of fast-flowing water can float many cars, since shallow moving water is deceptively powerful. Never drive through flooded roads.

quiz.q: The sudden calm during a cyclone means…
options: You may be in the eye; strong winds will return
quiz.why: A sudden calm in a cyclone may be the eye, and strong winds return soon after. Stay inside until the official all-clear.

quiz.q: After a flood, before switching on electricity…
quiz.why: After a flood, get the wiring checked before switching on power, because wet wiring can cause shocks and fires. Pouring water on sockets is dangerous.

quiz.q: Red warning from IMD means…
quiz.why: A red warning from IMD is the highest level and means take action. Ignoring it or just being aware is not enough.

scenes.text: In Dehradun, Kamla keeps a backpack by the door labelled ‘Go bag’. Her son Arush thinks it’s silly.
One night, a landslide alert asks their colony to evacuate in 20 minutes.
While neighbours search for torches and medicines, Kamla and Arush grab the bag, documents and grandma’s pills and leave in five minutes.
The family meets at the agreed spot and informs an uncle in Delhi, their out-of-town contact.

steps.title: What goes in a go-bag
steps.body:
- Drinking water and dry food (biscuits, chana, dry fruits) for 2–3 days
- Torch, spare batteries, power bank, whistle
- First-aid kit and **regular medicines** (with a prescription copy)
- Copies of documents (Aadhaar, insurance, bank details) in a waterproof pouch; digital copies in DigiLocker
- Some cash in small notes
- A change of clothes, raincoat, blanket, face masks, sanitary pads, baby items if needed
- List of important phone numbers on paper (phones die)

steps.title: A family emergency plan
steps.body:
1. **Meeting points**: one near home, one outside the neighbourhood.
2. **Out-of-town contact**: one relative everyone informs (local networks often jam).
3. **Who helps whom**: elderly, children, people with disabilities, pets.
4. **Know how to shut off** gas, electricity and water.
5. **School/office plans**: know their evacuation procedures.
6. **Practise** twice a year; update the bag (expiry dates) every six months.

steps.title: Important numbers
steps.body:
- **112**: all emergencies
- **101**: fire · **108**: ambulance in many states · **102**: ambulance/maternal in many states
- **1070** (state) / **1077** (district): disaster helplines in many states
- **1098**: Childline (children in need)
- **1930**: cyber fraud
- **14416**: Tele-MANAS mental health support
Save them in your phone and on paper.

steps.title: Don’t forget mind and community
steps.body: Disasters are frightening, especially for children. Explain plans calmly, give children small tasks, and check on neighbours who live alone. After a disaster, sleep problems and fear are common — talk about it, keep routines, and seek help (Tele-MANAS 14416) if distress continues.

activity.prompt: Build your go-bag and plan
items: Water and dry food for 2–3 days
Torch, batteries, whistle and power bank
Document copies in a waterproof pouch

quiz.q: Why keep a paper list of phone numbers?
options: Phones can die or be lost
quiz.why: Keep a paper list of phone numbers because phones can die or be lost, and batteries and networks fail in emergencies.

quiz.q: An out-of-town contact helps because…
options: Local networks may jam; one person can relay news
quiz.why: An out-of-town contact helps because local networks may jam, and long-distance calls or messages may still work, so one person can relay news.

quiz.q: How often should you check the go-bag?
quiz.why: Check the go-bag about every six months, because food, medicines and batteries expire. Leaving it for years or until after a disaster leaves you with useless supplies.

quiz.q: Tele-MANAS mental health helpline number is…
quiz.why: Tele-MANAS, the free national mental-health helpline, is 14416. 1077 is a disaster control line, 1906 is LPG and 101 is fire.

questions.why: During a fire, use the stairs, never the lift. Waiting on a balcony or hiding in a cupboard leaves you trapped.
Indoors in an earthquake, Drop, Cover and Hold On to protect your head and neck. Running out or standing by a window exposes you to falling objects and glass.
A go-bag should include regular medicines, because they are essential. A TV, heavy books and glass jars are bulky or fragile.
In PASS, the first P means Pull the pin, then Aim, Squeeze and Sweep. It does not mean pray or push.
If your clothes are on fire, stop, drop and roll to smother the flames. Running or fanning feeds the fire, and removing clothes while standing is too slow.
An orange IMD warning means be prepared. Red means take action, and ignoring a warning is unsafe.

questions.q: Why not walk through flood water?
options: Shallow moving water can knock you down, hide open drains, and carry live current
questions.why: Do not walk through flood water because shallow moving water can knock you down, hide open drains and carry live current. Many flood deaths happen this way.

questions.q: Water extinguisher on an electrical fire is…
questions.why: Using a water extinguisher on an electrical fire is dangerous because water conducts electricity and can shock you. Use an extinguisher meant for electrical fires.

options: A myth for most modern homes; Drop, Cover, Hold On is safer
questions.why: The 'doorway' advice is a myth for most modern homes, since doorways are not stronger and doors can swing. Drop, Cover, Hold On is safer.

questions.q: After a flood you develop fever after wading through water. Doctors may consider…
questions.why: A fever after wading through flood water may be leptospirosis, which spreads through water contaminated by animal urine, among other infections. Tell the doctor about the exposure.

questions.q: Fire in a flat: the door handle is hot. You should…
options: Keep it closed, seal gaps with wet cloth, signal from a window, call 112
questions.why: A hot door handle means fire behind it. Keep it closed, seal gaps with a wet cloth, signal from a window and call 112; opening it lets fire and smoke in.

questions.q: Cyclone eye passes; wind stops suddenly. Correct action?
questions.why: When a cyclone's eye passes the wind stops, but winds return from the opposite direction. Stay inside until the official all-clear; going out or driving is dangerous.

options: Go-bag + meeting points + out-of-town contact + shut-off knowledge + practice drills twice a year
questions.why: Layered planning works when stress is highest: a go-bag, meeting points, an out-of-town contact, knowledge of shut-offs and drills twice a year. Gold, phone-only records or prayer alone do not prepare a family.

questions.q: After an earthquake, trapped under debris. Which combination is best?
options: Cover mouth, avoid flames, tap on pipes/walls or whistle, conserve energy
Shout constantly and light a match to see
questions.why: Under debris, cover your mouth, avoid flames, tap pipes or walls or use a whistle, and conserve energy. This protects breathing, avoids igniting gas and signals efficiently, unlike kicking, shouting nonstop or lighting a match.
