courses.summary: Helmets, seatbelts, speed and phones; safety for pedestrians, cyclists and children; what to do at an accident scene, the golden hour and India’s Good Samaritan protections.
outcomes: Learners can explain why helmets, seatbelts and child seats save lives
Learners can walk and cycle more safely
Learners can secure an accident scene, call 112 and give basic help
Learners know Good Samaritans are legally protected in India
Learners know what to do after a minor crash

lessons.title: Helmets, seatbelts and speed

scenes.text: Varun, 17, rides pillion with his cousin to a shop two kilometres away in Patna. ‘No helmet, it’s just a short ride.’
A cow steps onto the road; the scooter skids. Varun’s head hits the kerb.
He survives with a serious head injury and months of recovery. His cousin, who wore a strapped helmet, has only bruises.
Varun now tells his school friends: ‘Most crashes happen close to home. Strap it, every time.’

steps.title: Why this matters
steps.body: Road crashes kill well over a lakh people in India every year, and a large share are young people and two-wheeler riders. Most crashes are preventable. Four big killers: **speeding, not wearing helmets, not wearing seatbelts, and drunk or distracted driving**.

steps.title: Helmets: wear it right
steps.body: Under the Motor Vehicles Act, helmets are compulsory for riders **and pillion riders** on two-wheelers (with limited exemptions such as for turban-wearing Sikhs). Choose a **BIS-certified (ISI-marked)** helmet that fits snugly, and **fasten the chin strap** — an unstrapped helmet flies off in a crash. Replace a helmet after any serious impact. Children on two-wheelers also need proper protection.

steps.title: Seatbelts and child seats
steps.body: Seatbelts are required for front **and rear** seats. In a crash, an unbelted rear passenger can be thrown forward with great force and injure themselves and those in front. Airbags work **with** seatbelts, not instead. Children should ride in the **back seat** in an age-appropriate child restraint; never hold a baby on your lap in a car.

steps.title: Speed and stopping distance
steps.body:
Stopping distance = **reaction distance** + **braking distance**. In about 1 second of reaction time:
- At 36 km/h you travel 10 m before even braking.
- At 72 km/h you travel 20 m — and braking distance roughly **quadruples** when speed doubles.
So a small speed increase makes a big difference in crash force and stopping. Slow down near schools, markets, curves, at night, and in rain or fog.

steps.title: Underage driving
steps.body: In India, you can get a learner’s licence for a gearless two-wheeler up to 50 cc at **16** (with parent/guardian consent), and for other vehicles at **18**. Driving without a licence is illegal and dangerous; the Motor Vehicles Act provides strict penalties when a juvenile commits an offence, including for the guardian or owner of the vehicle.

statements.s: Pillion riders on two-wheelers must also wear helmets.
statements.why: The law and physics apply to both.

statements.s: An unstrapped helmet protects just as well.
statements.why: It can come off before impact.

statements.s: Rear-seat passengers in cars need seatbelts too.
statements.why: Unbelted rear passengers are thrown forward in crashes.

statements.s: Airbags make seatbelts unnecessary.
statements.why: Airbags are designed to work with seatbelts.

statements.s: Doubling speed roughly quadruples braking distance.
statements.why: Braking distance grows with the square of speed.

quiz.q: A good helmet in India should be…
quiz.why: A good helmet should be BIS-certified (ISI mark) and properly strapped. A loose helmet, a cap or a decorative one will not protect in a crash.

quiz.q: Where should young children sit in a car?
options: On an adult’s lap in front
In the back seat in a suitable child restraint
quiz.why: Young children are safest in the back seat in a suitable child restraint. Standing, sitting on a lap or on the dashboard can be fatal in a crash.

quiz.q: At 72 km/h, distance travelled in 1 second is about…
quiz.why: Convert units: 72 km/h = 72 × 1000 ÷ 3600 = 20 m/s, so you travel about 20 m in 1 second.

quiz.q: Minimum age to get a learner’s licence for most motor vehicles (non-gearless ≤50cc) in India?
quiz.why: The minimum age is 18 for most vehicles; 16 applies only to gearless two-wheelers up to 50 cc with consent. 14 and 21 are not the thresholds.

sources: WHO Global status report on road safety

scenes.text: Ten-year-old twins Ira and Ilan in Pune walk to school. Ilan always looks at his phone while crossing.
One day a car turning left nearly hits him. The driver hadn’t seen him behind a parked van.
Their grandfather teaches them: stop, look right-left-right, listen, and cross only when sure — never from behind parked vehicles.
On weekends they cycle with helmets and bright clothes, and a light on the cycle after dusk.

steps.title: Crossing the road (India drives on the left)
steps.body:
1. Find a safe place: zebra crossing, signal, footbridge or subway.
2. **Stop** at the kerb.
3. **Look right, left, then right again** (traffic nearest you comes from the right in India); **listen**.
4. Make **eye contact** with drivers.
5. Cross straight, **walk, don’t run**, keep looking.
6. Never cross from between parked vehicles or at bends.
In countries that drive on the right (USA, much of Europe), look left first.

steps.title: Be seen
steps.body:
- Walk on the footpath; if none, walk **facing oncoming traffic** on the edge.
- Wear light or reflective clothes at night; carry a torch.
- **Put the phone and earphones away** while crossing.
- Hold small children’s hands; they can’t judge speed and distance well until around age 10.

steps.title: Cycling rules of thumb
steps.body:
- Wear a helmet; check brakes, tyres, chain, bell.
- Ride on the left, in a straight line; don’t weave between vehicles.
- Use hand signals before turning.
- Front white light and rear red light/reflector at night.
- Stay out of large vehicles’ **blind spots** — if you can’t see the driver in their mirror, they can’t see you. Never ride alongside a turning truck or bus.

steps.title: Common danger moments
steps.body:
- Vehicles turning left at junctions (they cut across your path).
- Car doors opening suddenly (‘dooring’) — keep a door’s width away from parked cars.
- Wet roads, potholes and open drains in monsoon.
- Reversing vehicles in parking lots — children are hard to see.

activity.prompt: Put the safe road-crossing steps in order (India).
items: Look right, left, then right again and listen

quiz.q: In India, when crossing, look first to the…
quiz.why: India drives on the left, so the traffic nearest you comes from the right. Look right first, then left, then right again before crossing.

quiz.q: If there’s no footpath, walk…
quiz.why: With no footpath, walk facing oncoming traffic so you can see what is coming and move away. Walking with your back to it hides danger.

quiz.q: Why avoid riding beside a turning truck?
options: You may be in the driver’s blind spot
quiz.why: A turning truck's driver has blind spots and may not see you beside the vehicle. That is why you should not ride next to it.

quiz.q: At night, a cyclist should have…
options: Front white light and rear red light/reflector
quiz.why: At night a cyclist needs a front white light and a rear red light or reflector, because visibility prevents crashes. Dark clothes and no lights make you hard to see.

lessons.title: At an accident scene: the golden hour and Good Samaritans

scenes.text: On the Mumbai–Pune expressway, Neha and her father see a car that has hit the divider. People are slowing down to film.
Her father parks safely ahead, turns on hazard lights, and Neha calls 112 with the kilometre marker.
A woman in the car is conscious but bleeding from the arm. Neha presses a clean cloth on it; her father keeps the driver still because he complains of neck pain.
Police thank them and let them go after a simple statement. Neha learns that the law protects people who help.

steps.title: Secure, call, care
steps.body:
1. **Secure**: park safely, hazard lights on, warning triangle or people waving traffic down well behind the scene. Switch off the crashed vehicle’s engine if you can safely; no smoking.
2. **Call 112** (or 108): exact location (landmark, kilometre stone, live location), number of injured, their state.
3. **Care**: talk to the injured, keep them warm and calm; control bleeding with direct pressure; CPR if not breathing normally.
4. **Don’t move** injured people unless there is immediate danger (fire, traffic) — neck or spine may be hurt. Don’t remove a motorcyclist’s helmet unless they aren’t breathing and you need to open the airway.
5. Don’t give food or water.

steps.title: The golden hour
steps.body: The **golden hour** is the period shortly after a traumatic injury when prompt medical care gives the best chance of survival. The Motor Vehicles Act (as amended in 2019) defines it as one hour following a traumatic injury and provides for a scheme for cashless treatment of road accident victims during this period. Fast calling and helping the ambulance find the spot can save a life.

steps.title: You are protected: Good Samaritan law
steps.body:
A **Good Samaritan** is a person who, in good faith and without expecting payment, helps an injured person at an accident. **Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act** (inserted in 2019) and guidelines approved by the Supreme Court (2016) say:
- A Good Samaritan **shall not be liable** for any civil or criminal action for injury or death of the victim caused by negligence in acting or failing to act while helping in good faith.
- You **can’t be forced to give your name** or personal details to police or hospital.
- Hospitals should not demand payment or delay emergency treatment because you brought the victim.
- Being a witness is voluntary.

steps.title: Don’t be a spectator
steps.body: Filming or crowding blocks ambulances and violates the victim’s dignity. If you can’t help directly, help by calling 112, directing traffic safely, or making space.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. Laws and schemes are updated from time to time; first-aid training makes you a far more effective helper.

a.text: You see a motorcyclist lying on the road after a crash. Traffic is still moving. What first?

choices.label: Run into the road immediately
choices.feedback: You could be hit too. Danger first.

choices.label: Make the scene safe: get others to slow traffic, then approach
choices.feedback: Correct — safety first.

b.text: He is conscious, groaning, says his neck hurts. His leg is bleeding.

choices.label: Remove his helmet to make him comfortable and sit him up
choices.feedback: Moving the head could worsen a spine injury.

choices.label: Call 112, keep him still, press a cloth firmly on the bleeding
choices.feedback: Exactly.

c.text: At the hospital, staff ask for your phone number and address. You don’t want to share.

choices.label: Politely say you are a Good Samaritan and choose not to share personal details
choices.feedback: That’s your right under the Good Samaritan provisions.

choices.label: Leave without informing anyone
choices.feedback: You may leave, but informing staff about what happened helps the victim’s treatment.

bad.text: That increased risk. Remember: secure the scene, call 112, don’t move the injured unless there’s danger, control bleeding.

good.text: You helped save a life within the golden hour — and the law protects you.

quiz.q: First step at a road accident scene?
options: Move the injured to your car immediately
quiz.why: First make the scene safe, for example by warning traffic, to prevent further crashes. Moving the injured, removing helmets or filming comes later or is wrong.

quiz.q: Can police force a Good Samaritan to give personal details?
quiz.why: No, disclosure is voluntary for a Good Samaritan, under the Good Samaritan guidelines. Police cannot force a helper to give personal details.

quiz.q: Which section of the Motor Vehicles Act protects Good Samaritans?
quiz.why: Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act, inserted in 2019, protects Good Samaritans. 302 and 420 are IPC sections and 1A is not relevant.

quiz.q: Why not remove an injured rider’s helmet routinely?
options: It may worsen a neck/spine injury
quiz.why: Do not routinely remove an injured rider's helmet because it may worsen a neck or spine injury. Remove it only if needed to open the airway.

quiz.q: The ‘golden hour’ refers to…
options: The period after injury when prompt care most improves survival
quiz.why: The 'golden hour' is the period after injury when prompt care most improves survival. It has nothing to do with sunset, lunch or traffic.

sources: Motor Vehicles Act 1988, sections 2(12A) and 134A (2019 amendment)
Supreme Court — Save Life Foundation v. Union of India (2016)

lessons.title: Phones, drinking, tiredness — and after a minor crash

scenes.text: Driving home in Jaipur, Akash glances at a WhatsApp message for ‘just two seconds’.
He rear-ends a scooter at a signal. Luckily the rider is only shaken.
They move to the side, take photos, exchange details and insurance information, and Akash apologises.
Akash now keeps his phone in the glovebox — ‘Do Not Disturb while driving’ is permanently on.

steps.title: Distraction
steps.body: At 60 km/h a car moves about 17 metres every second. A 2-second glance at a phone = 33 metres driven blind. Using a handheld phone while driving is an offence in India. Hands-free calls still distract the mind. Use ‘Do Not Disturb while driving’, set navigation before starting, and pull over safely if you must use the phone.

steps.title: Alcohol and drugs
steps.body: In India the legal limit is **30 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood** for drivers; drink-driving carries heavy fines and possible imprisonment, and penalties increase for repeat offences. Even small amounts slow reaction time and judgement. Some medicines (for allergies, sleep, pain) cause drowsiness — read the label. Plan ahead: designated sober driver, cab, or stay over. Never ride with a drunk driver.

steps.title: Tiredness kills
steps.body: Drowsy driving causes many highway crashes, especially between midnight and dawn and after lunch. Warning signs: yawning, heavy eyelids, drifting lanes, missing exits. Coffee and open windows don’t fix it. **Stop safely and rest**; take a break about every 2 hours on long drives; share driving.

steps.title: After a minor crash
steps.body:
1. Stop safely; hazard lights on; check for injuries; call 112 if anyone is hurt.
2. Stay calm; don’t argue or admit fault in anger.
3. Take **photos**: vehicles, number plates, positions, road, damage.
4. Exchange names, phone numbers, vehicle registration and insurance details.
5. Inform your **insurer promptly** (many have a time limit).
6. If someone is injured, there is a dispute, or for certain claims, report to the police; an FIR or police report may be needed.
7. Keep repair bills and medical records.

steps.title: Keep your papers ready
steps.body: Carry (or keep in DigiLocker / mParivahan) your driving licence, registration certificate, valid insurance and PUC certificate. Digital documents from these official apps are accepted by traffic authorities.

activity.prompt: A car moves at 54 km/h. The driver looks at a phone for 3 seconds. How many metres does the car travel ‘blind’? (54 km/h = 15 m/s)

quiz.q: Legal blood-alcohol limit for drivers in India?
quiz.why: The legal blood-alcohol limit for drivers in India is 30 mg per 100 ml of blood. 80 mg is the limit in some other countries.

quiz.q: Best cure for drowsiness while driving?
quiz.why: The only cure for drowsiness is to stop safely and rest, since only sleep fixes sleepiness. An open window or loud music gives a brief lift, and driving faster adds risk.

quiz.q: After a minor crash, first check…
quiz.why: After a minor crash, first check whether anyone is injured, because people come before cars or phones.

quiz.q: Digital driving licence and RC in DigiLocker/mParivahan are…
quiz.why: Digital driving licences and RCs in DigiLocker or mParivahan are official documents and are accepted by traffic authorities. They are valid in India, not illegal.

questions.q: Helmet rule for pillion riders in India?
questions.why: Both the rider and the pillion must wear helmets. It is not optional or limited to night or highways.

questions.q: When crossing in India, look first…
questions.why: Traffic nearest you comes from the right because India drives on the left, so look right first.
At an accident, dial 112, the all-emergency number. 155260 and 1930 are cyber fraud lines and 1906 is LPG.

questions.q: A child under the safe age to judge traffic should…
questions.why: A young child should hold an adult's hand because children cannot judge speed and distance well. Crossing alone, running or using earphones is unsafe.

questions.q: Do rear-seat car passengers need seatbelts?
questions.why: Yes, rear-seat passengers need seatbelts too; it is required and life-saving. Unbelted rear passengers can be thrown forward and injure themselves and others.

questions.q: Good Samaritans in India are protected under MV Act section…
questions.why: Good Samaritans are protected under Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act. The other numbers are unrelated.
Stopping distance is reaction distance (while you notice and respond) plus braking distance. Both add up.

questions.q: Why stay a door’s width from parked cars when cycling?
questions.why: Keep a door's width from parked cars so you are not hit by a suddenly opened door; 'dooring' crashes are common.

questions.q: A conscious crash victim has neck pain. You should…
questions.why: A conscious crash victim with neck pain may have a spine injury, so keep them still and call 112. Walking, sitting up or giving water could worsen it.

questions.q: At 90 km/h, a 2-second glance covers about…
questions.why: 90 km/h = 90 ÷ 3.6 = 25 m/s, so in 2 seconds you travel 25 × 2 = 50 m.

questions.q: Hospital refuses to treat an accident victim until the helper pays a deposit. Under Good Samaritan guidelines…
options: Helpers shouldn’t be made to pay or be detained; emergency care shouldn’t be delayed
questions.why: Under Good Samaritan guidelines, helpers should not be made to pay or be detained, and emergency care should not be delayed. The guidelines protect helpers and the victim's access to care.

questions.q: If braking distance at 40 km/h is about 8 m, at 80 km/h it is roughly…
questions.why: Braking distance grows with the square of speed, so doubling from 40 to 80 km/h makes it about 4 times: 8 × 4 = 32 m.

questions.q: Which plan for a party night is safest?
options: Designated sober driver or cab; never ride with a drunk driver
questions.why: Only zero alcohol before driving is safe, so use a designated sober driver or a cab and never ride with a drunk driver. Coffee, open windows or driving slowly do not remove impairment.

questions.q: Correct priority at a highway crash with fuel leaking and one unresponsive victim not breathing?
options: Wait for police before touching anything
Light a flare near the fuel
Secure scene/warn traffic, call 112, if fire risk move victim only as needed for safety, start CPR
questions.why: Danger comes first: secure the scene and warn traffic, call 112, move the victim only if there is an immediate fire risk, and start CPR if they are not breathing. Do not light a flare near fuel, film or wait while someone is not breathing.

objects.label: Pulp

steps.title: Two kinds of digestion
steps.body: Mechanical digestion breaks food into small pieces (chewing, churning). Chemical digestion uses enzymes to break molecules into small nutrients.

steps.title: Peristalsis
steps.body: Food moves through your gut by wave-like muscle contractions - you can swallow even upside-down.

objects.label: Mouth
objects.info: Teeth chew food (mechanical digestion). Saliva contains amylase which starts breaking down starch.

objects.label: Oesophagus
objects.info: A muscular tube about 25 cm long. Waves of muscle contraction (peristalsis) push food to the stomach.

objects.label: Stomach
objects.info: Churns food with acid (pH about 1.5-3.5) and the enzyme pepsin, which begins protein digestion.

objects.label: Liver
objects.info: Makes bile, processes nutrients and detoxifies the blood. The largest internal organ.

objects.label: Gall bladder
objects.info: Stores and concentrates bile, released to help digest fats.

objects.label: Pancreas
objects.info: Makes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate that go to the small intestine, plus insulin for blood sugar.

objects.label: Small intestine
objects.info: About 6 m long (in life). Final chemical digestion and nearly all nutrient absorption happen here, through finger-like villi.

objects.label: Large intestine
objects.info: About 1.5 m long. Absorbs water and salts, hosts gut bacteria and forms faeces.

objects.label: Rectum and anus
objects.info: Store and eliminate waste.

steps.title: Three particles
steps.body: Protons (+1), neutrons (0), electrons (-1). An atom is neutral when protons equal electrons.

steps.title: Mostly empty
steps.body: If the nucleus were a pea in the middle of a stadium, the electrons would be at the stands - an atom is mostly empty space.

activity.prompt: Find protons, neutrons and electrons and note their charges.

objects.label: Protons
objects.info: Positively charged particles in the nucleus. Carbon has 6 protons - that number is its atomic number and defines the element.

objects.label: Neutrons
objects.info: Neutral particles in the nucleus with about the same mass as a proton. Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons.

objects.label: Nucleus
objects.info: Tiny, dense core holding protons and neutrons - about 100,000 times smaller than the atom, yet it has nearly all the mass.

objects.label: K shell (n=1)
objects.info: First shell, holds up to 2 electrons.

objects.label: L shell (n=2)
objects.info: Second shell, holds up to 8 electrons. Carbon has 4 here - its valence electrons - so it forms four bonds.

objects.label: Electron (K)
objects.info: Negatively charged, about 1/1836 the mass of a proton.

objects.label: Electron (K, second)
objects.info: Electrons in the same shell repel each other, so they stay on opposite sides.

objects.label: Valence electron 1
objects.info: Outer (valence) electrons take part in bonding.

objects.label: Valence electron 2
objects.info: Carbon needs four more electrons for a full outer shell.

objects.label: Valence electron 3
objects.info: Sharing electrons creates covalent bonds.

objects.label: Valence electron 4
objects.info: Four valence electrons make carbon uniquely versatile: diamond, graphite, DNA and fuels.

objects.info: The pair is attracted to both nuclei - a covalent bond. Bond length in H2 is about 74 pm.

objects.label: Metal ion 1
objects.info: In a metal, atoms lose valence electrons and become positive ions in a lattice.

objects.label: Metal ion 2
objects.info: Ions are fixed in a regular arrangement.

objects.label: Metal ion 3
objects.info: Metals are malleable because layers can slide without breaking the electron sea.

objects.label: Metal ion 4
objects.info: The electrons are delocalised.

objects.label: Sea of electrons
objects.info: Delocalised electrons move freely, so metals conduct heat and electricity and are shiny.
